title: Hy Nguyen, Maghsoodloo, Grischuk Take 3 0 Thursday Titles
summary: GM Parham Maghsoodloo scored in the top four in three different 3 0 Thursday Tournaments on October 1. His nine points in the first tournament weren't quite enough to win, as he took second on tiebreaks behind IM Quoc Hy Nguyen. Maghsoodloo dominated the second event, winning with the day's best score, 10 points. In the third tournament, he had to settle for playing spoiler, defeating IM Reza Mahdavi in the final game, handing first place to GM Alexander Grischuk. Heading into the final round of the first tournament, Maghsoodloo, GM Tuan Minh Le, and GM Alexey Sarana led the tournament with 8.5 points. Sarana fell to a strong attack by GM Denis Lazavik, while Maghsoodloo faced Minh Le.

title: Bluebaum Takes First Freestyle Friday Of New Season
summary: GM Matthias Bluebaum won the return tournament of Freestyle Friday on October 2 with nine points, taking the tournament outright ahead of GMs Oleksandr Bortnyk, Pranav Venkatesh, and SL Narayanan on 8.5/11. Pranav clinched an appearance in next year's Freestyle World Championship earlier in the year, but the start to the October-December season was even better for the other three as they jockey for position in the knockout tournament that will determine other qualifiers. James Dash and GM Vidit Gujrathi commentated on the proceedings, which you can view here: Several top players lost in the first few rounds, but Bortnyk, GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda, and IM Renato Terry remained perfect through four rounds. Duda got there remaining in control against GM Rasmus Svane... except for one move, but Svane missed the chance. Duda's conversion wasn't easy, but Svane eventually cracked.

title: Freestyle Friday Returns With World Championship Spots On The Line
summary: Freestyle Friday returns to Chess.com this Friday, October 2, resuming the race for places in the 2027 FIDE Freestyle Chess World Championships. Ten weekly tournaments remain before December's knockout finals, which will award one qualification spot in each of the Open and Women's fields. GMs Magnus Carlsen, Fabiano Caruana, Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Vincent Keymer, and Pranav Venkatesh have already qualified for the Open championship. Three of the eight places remain available in each field. Alongside the Freestyle Friday qualification spots, two further online qualifiers will give players opportunities to reach Weissenhaus, Germany, where both championships will take place in February. GMs Hans Niemann, Denis Lazavik, Ian Nepomniachtchi, and Nodirbek Yakubboev are among the players expected to compete in the first event after the three-month break, organizers say. GMs Anna Muzychuk and Alexandra Kosteniuk are also expected to take part. Friday's event begins at 11 a.m. ET / 5 p.m. CEST / 8:30 p.m. IST, with live coverage on Chess.com, the Freestyle Chess YouTube channel, and DAZN. "Formula One has its Grand Prix weekends. Chess now has its Fridays. With Freestyle Friday and our online qualifiers, the road to a World Championship becomes a season-long show. That's the future of the game," Freestyle Chess CEO Dr. Andreas Walker said in a press release. The weekly broadcasts will feature hosts who compete while commentating on their games. The announced lineup includes GMs Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Niemann, Vidit Gujrathi, and Oleksandr Bortnyk, along with WFM Anna Cramling, WGM Dina Belenkaya, and ChessBase India's IM Sagar Shah and GM Harshit Raja. Freestyle Friday is an 11-round Swiss tournament for titled players, played with a 3+2 time control. Freestyle chess, also known as Chess960 or Fischer Random, randomizes the starting arrangement of the back-rank pieces, reducing players' reliance on memorized opening preparation. The championship resumes with an important detail, announced by FIDE and Freestyle Friday in August: points earned during the first half of the season carry over. Players will continue adding to their totals every Friday through December 4, with separate Open and Women's leaderboards. Weekly points range from 10 for first place to one for eighth through 10th. The top seven eligible players in each field will advance to a knockout stage. The quarterfinals take place on December 11, followed by the semifinals and finals on December 18. The winner in each field earns a World Championship spot. Pranav and Muzychuk have already qualified through the first half of the Freestyle Friday Championship. Pranav topped the Open standings with 60 points, while Muzychuk led the Women's standings with 88:

title: From Tsaghkadzor to Grand Final: European Schools Chess Champions crowned amidst cultural celebration
summary: The curtain fell on the World Schools Team Championship Europe 2026. After four days of intense competition, brilliant sacrifices, and unparalleled teamwork, the young chess champions were crowned in Tsaghkadzor, Armenia. Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk (Belarus) established their dominance from the opening round. Starting with back-to-back 4–0 clean sweeps, they held a firm grasp on the number-one spot. Led by Board 1 star Damir Bulgak and Board 4 standout Katrina Yakovleva, the Belarusian squad never let their grip slip, successfully turning away all challengers to finish with a flawless, undefeated record. Their first-place finish officially secures their slot in the prestigious global Grand Final this December. Coming into the event as the top-seeded team by average rating, Riga State Gymnasium No. 1 (Latvia) confidently navigated eight rounds, losing only to the champions and winning all their other encounters.  Powered by Daniel Beniosev’s unbeaten run on Board 2, the Latvians easily defended their position down the stretch to lock up the silver medals. LEPL Georgia, Kutaisi Andria Razmadze Physico secured the third position in a tough competition with the local team from Armenia. Final standings Let’s take a look at how the action unfolded on the final day of the competition. Round 7 Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk further consolidated its lead, scoring a hard-fought victory over ZS Wolkerova Bardejov. Meanwhile, in the clash of the teams chasing the leaders, Riga State Gymnasium No. 1 dominated LEPL Georgia, Kutaisi Andria Razmadze Physico by a score of 3-1. Move of the day Matej Viglas – Damir Bulgak Leading up to move 26, Black emerged clearly better, but there was nothing decisive in sight after the correct 26.Ne5 f6 27.Nd3. However, White committed a fatal error with 26. Nd2??, walking right into a devastating tactical strike. The knight sacrifice 26… Nxf2! completely shattered White’s kingside shelter. Accepting the sacrifice leads to a forced checkmate after 27.Kxf2 Qxh2+ 28.Kf1 Re6!, while declining it leaves White completely lost. The rest was smooth sailing for Bulgak. Round 8 Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk finished with a perfect match score after defeating Green Village School of Israel. Riga State Gymnasium No.1 swept Osnovna sola Bojana Ilicha Maribor, while in the crucial match for third place LEPL Georgia, Kutaisi Andria Razmadze Physico prevailed over the local team Yerevan’s basic school N 77. A web of friendships Beyond the intense chess battles on the chessboards of Tsaghkadzor, the World Schools Team Championship 2026 celebrated the power of global connection through a deeply symbolic “Threads that connect” side event. In this heartwarming activity, young chess prodigies from across Europe stood in a large circle, sharing their reflections and tossing colorful balls of yarn across the room while holding onto their piece of the string. As the yarn traveled from hand to hand, it created a magnificent, intricate web, a striking, tangible visualization of international networking and shared community. This playful yet profound exercise beautifully reminded our future grandmasters that just like their strategic choices on the board, their paths, cultures, and newfound friendships are all interconnected in one grand, supportive network. School Champions crowned in Tsaghkadzor amid tears, triumphs, and anthems. The European Stage World Schools Team Championship 2026 concluded with an unforgettable, high-energy closing ceremony hosted at the 88 Hotel & Spa. Bringing together young players, captains, parents, and international chess dignitaries, the event celebrated four days of intense boundary-crossing competition, ultimate triumphs, and cross-cultural camaraderie. The Master of Ceremonies opened the evening by thanking the young players for building friendships across borders, emphasizing that the global chess community is “one big family.” Special recognition was paid to Freedom Group of companies, the event’s main sponsor and General Partner of the International School Chess Federation (ISCF). The MC also expressed deep appreciation to the tournament’s key co-organizers: the Armenian Chess Federation, the Chess Academy of Armenia, the European Chess Union, and the venue host, 88 Hotel & Spa. The official segment of the evening began with the national anthem of Armenia. The audience remained respectfully standing before the proceedings transitioned seamlessly into the official FIDE anthem. Following the protocols, the energy in the hall skyrocketed during the screening of the tournament’s highlight film, titled “How It All Happened.” Young players filled the room with thunderous shouts and laughter, following the MC’s prompt to “make some noise” whenever they spotted themselves on screen. Individual board triumphs Chief Arbiter Vahagn Khachatryan took the stage to announce the individual category medalists, who were presented their awards by an esteemed lineup of academic and chess royalty. Reserve Board awards were presented by Mariam Ispiryan, Pro-rector of the Armenian State Pedagogical University. Lile Svanadze  from LEPL Georgia, Kutaisi Andria Razmadze Physico-Mathematical Public School N41 Catalan Julen Arbizu  from Ikastola San Fermin Maksymilian Wylezinski  from Azymut Szkola Podstawowa Fundacji Sternik Board 4 awards were presented by Grandmaster and Honored Coach of Armenia, Arman Pashikyan.  loana-Cristiana Pomirleanu from C.N. Costache Negruzzi Katrina Yakovleva  from Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk Adam Ben Avi  from Green Village School Board 3 awards were presented by Varduhi Sargsyan, Executive Director of the Chess Academy of Armenia Krisjanis Lazars from Riga State Gymnasium No. 1 Platon Kiritshenko from Tallinna Tonismae Reaalkool Kiryl Babeikin from Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk Board 2 awards were presented by Lilit Mkrtchyan, Rector of the Armenian State Pedagogical University Daniel Beniosev from Riga State Gymnasium No. 1 Mikita Mazanik from Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk Adrian Kornilov from Tallinna Tonismae Reaalkool Board 1 awards were presented by Ion-Serban Dobronauteanu, Director of Youth Chess of the European Chess Union. title: Small Nations Chess Association restarts activities and elects new Board
summary: Members of the Small Nations Chess Association (SNACA) convened in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, for the Association’s General Assembly, where they agreed to revitalize SNACA’s operations, approved new statutes, and elected a new Board to serve a two-year term. SNACA now includes 35 member federations from four continents, reflecting the growing international community of chess federations represented within the Association. As part of its renewed agenda, SNACA is planning to organize its first individual championship in 2027, marking an important milestone in the Association’s development and future activities. The General Assembly in Samarkand represents a new chapter for SNACA as it continues to strengthen cooperation among small nations and provide opportunities for their chess communities to participate in international events. title: Upcoming tournaments and events
summary:
The following tournament information was provided for us by MyChess.Events , a global portal that tracks over-the-board chess tournaments worldwide. On its description pages you will find format, date, schedules, prize funds, etc. The site also helps players find registration details, schedules, venues, and organizer information.

November 2-15 | Vrnjačka Banja, Serbia

One of the most important official senior events of the year. Four world titles will be decided in Open 50+, Women 50+, Open 65+, and Women 65+, with 11 rounds of classical chess and a €50,000 total prize fund. Vrnjačka Banja has developed into an important international chess destination.

Full information at MyChess .

November 2–13 | Hersonissos, Crete, Greece

A major ECU championship bringing together young players from across Europe in twelve Open and Girls categories from U8 to U18. The event offers nine rounds of classical chess and combines a serious continental championship with the strong destination appeal of Crete.

Full information at MyChess .

November 4-9 | Bellevue, Washington, USA

The 20th edition of one of the best-known American norm tournaments, a nine-round FIDE- and US Chess-rated event with GM, IM, WGM, and WIM norm possibilities, a $12,500 prize fund, and additional rapid and blitz events. Particularly attractive for ambitious titled players and norm seekers.

Full information at MyChess .

November 9-17 | Dushanbe, Tajikistan

After a successful inaugural edition, the President’s Cup returns with an increased $60,000 prize fund and separate groups for players rated above and below 2200. It is one of the largest international chess events currently being developed in Tajikistan.

Full information at MyChess .

November 10-17 | Batumi, Georgia

This is the final stage of FIDE’s new World Cadets Championship cycle for U8, U10, and U12 players. Only 48 qualified finalists will compete across six Open and Girls categories, making it a very selective world championship rather than a large open-entry youth tournament.

Full information at MyChess .

November 11-16 | Sinacaban, Misamis Occidental, Philippines

A new international event with a very deep $37,700 prize fund. The nine-round FIDE-rated Swiss offers possible title norms depending on the final field, while prizes extend all the way through 30th place together with numerous special categories.

Full information at MyChess .

November 17-28 | Greater Caracas, Venezuela

One of FIDE’s most important junior championships, with separate Open and Girls U20 competitions over 11 classical rounds. The event brings leading young players from national federations around the world to Caracas and offers both FIDE title and norm opportunities.

Full information at MyChess .

Nov. 24-29 | Garden Grove, California, USA

A historic Thanksgiving-week tournament now reaching its 61st edition. The American Open offers six playing sections, a guaranteed $40,000 prize fund, FIDE rating in the top sections, and possible title norms in the Championship. The wider festival also includes scholastic chess, blitz, action chess, lectures, and a GM simul.

Full information at MyChess .

November 25-29 | Charlotte, North Carolina, USA

The US Masters is a US Chess National Championship with a $27,500 guaranteed prize fund, GM/IM/WGM/WIM norm opportunities, and FIDE Circuit 2026–2027 status. Its strong single-section field should make it especially relevant for people interested in high-level competitive chess.

Full information at MyChess.

November 28 - December 5 | Benidorm, Alicante, Spain

A long-established Spanish international open and the main Open A event of the Gran Hotel Bali Chess Festival. The tournament offers nine FIDE-rated classical rounds, title-norm possibilities, and €16,800 in Open A cash prizes.

Full information at MyChess .

title: Jon Speelman at 70: A leading figure of English chess
summary:
British champion, Candidates semifinalist, author and analyst

Grandmaster Jonathan Speelman turns 70 on 2 October 2026. One of the leading English players of the 1980s and early 1990s, Speelman reached the Candidates semifinals, climbed as high as joint fourth in the world rankings and represented England throughout one of the most successful periods in the country's chess history. His career combined strong results in individual tournaments, repeated success in national competition, two appearances in the Candidates and a long record in team events, while his later work as an author, columnist and analyst made him a familiar figure well beyond tournament play.

Jonathan Simon Speelman was born on 2 October 1956 in Marylebone, London. He attended St Paul's School and later studied mathematics at Worcester College, Oxford, a background that fitted naturally with the analytical character of his chess. Speelman left Oxford in 1977 and turned to chess professionally. His progress was rapid: he was awarded the international master (IM) title in 1978 and became a grandmaster (GM) in 1980, at a time when England was beginning to produce a particularly strong generation of players.

Speelman's peak years came towards the end of the 1980s. His highest FIDE rating was 2645, achieved in July 1988, when he stood fifth in the world. By January 1989 his rating had slipped slightly to 2640, but his ranking had improved to joint fourth , the highest position of his career. That distinction is worth noting, since his peak rating and peak ranking came on different rating lists. At the time, he competed in elite events and in the World Championship cycle at a level reached by few English players before or since.

January 1989 FIDE ranking | Source: OlimpBase

Early achievements and British titles

Speelman had already established himself as one of Britain's most promising young players before reaching adulthood. He won the British Under-14 Championship in 1969 and shared first place in the British Under-16 Championship in 1970. Those results were followed by steady progress through the national and international ranks, and by the late 1970s he was already competing successfully at senior level. In 1978, the same year in which he received the IM title, he won his first British Championship and was also part of the England team that won the World Under-26 Team Championship in Mexico City, finishing ahead of the Soviet Union.

He returned to the top of the British Championship later in the following decade, winning the title again in 1985 and 1986. The three national victories came during a notably competitive period in English chess, when players such as Tony Miles, John Nunn and Nigel Short were regularly active at a high international level. Speelman's British titles thus were achieved within a national scene that was itself unusually strong.

Jon Speelman at the 1982 Chess Olympiad in Lucerne | Photo: Krtschil via Wikimedia Commons

The English team at the 1986 Dubai Chess Olympiad: Jon Speelman, Nigel Short, John Nunn and Tony Miles | Photo: Gerhard Hund via Wikimedia Commons

International results and the Candidates

Speelman compiled a series of notable international tournament results during the 1980s. He shared first place at Dortmund in 1981, then did the same at Hastings in 1983/84. He returned to Hastings to share first again in 1986/87, this time going through the event undefeated. In 1987 he also shared first place at Be'er Sheva, where he scored 8½/11 without losing a game. Results of this kind, together with his rising rating, helped place him securely among the leading grandmasters of the period and provided the platform for his strongest run in the World Championship cycle.

That run began at the 1987 Subotica Interzonal, one of the qualifying tournaments for the Candidates. Speelman shared first place with Gyula Sax and Nigel Short, thereby securing a place in the Candidates. The field included a number of established international stars.

In the first round of the Candidates he faced the American grandmaster Yasser Seirawan and won convincingly by 4-1. The quarterfinal brought an all-English match against Nigel Short. Speelman won 3½-1½ and advanced to the semifinals, one of the best individual achievements of his career. There he faced Jan Timman, one of the strongest players of the era. The match was much closer, with Timman eventually prevailing 4½-3½.

Jon Speelman and Nigel Short during their 1989 Candidates match | Photo: British Chess News

His performance in that cycle also gave him a place in the Candidates of the following World Championship cycle. Once again he met Short, but this time the result was reversed: Short won by 5½-4½.

Cycle Stage Opponent Place Date Result

1987–90 First round Yasser Seirawan Saint John, Canada January 1988 Won 4–1

1987–90 Quarterfinal Nigel Short London, England August 1988 Won 3½–1½

1987–90 Semifinal Jan Timman London, England October 1989 Lost 3½–4½

1990–93 First round Nigel Short London, England January-February 1991 Lost 4½–5½

All games - Speelman at the Candidates

Team achievements and work beyond tournament play

Speelman was also a major figure in England's national team for more than two decades. He played in every Chess Olympiad from 1980 through 2006, an unusually long sequence of appearances.

His strongest period with the team coincided with England's best run of Olympiad results: silver medals at Thessaloniki in 1984, Dubai in 1986 and Thessaloniki again in 1988, each time behind the Soviet Union. At Dubai 1986, Speelman scored 7/9 as first reserve, with five wins and four draws, and received an individual silver medal for his performance. Two years later, playing on board two, he scored 8½/12, another of his strongest results in Olympiad competition. He also recorded 8/12 at both Novi Sad 1990 and Moscow 1994.

In 1997, he was part of the England team that won the European Team Championship in Pula, alongside Nigel Short, Michael Adams, Matthew Sadler and Julian Hodgson.

Jon Speelman at a four-hander blitz challenge - with Alexei Shirov and two kids - organised by Gibtelecom in 2005: Shirov/Andreev v. Speelman/Erding (0-1) | Photos: John Saunders

Away from competitive play, Speelman developed a substantial parallel career as a chess writer, commentator and analyst. He has been particularly associated with endgame analysis, and his books include Analysing the Endgame , Endgame Preparation and, as co-author, Batsford Chess Endings . He also wrote extensively for the British press, including work for The Observer and The Independent .

Speelman's analytical reputation has long been one of the defining features of his chess career, complementing a playing style known for unconventional strategic ideas and tactical resourcefulness.

At 70, Speelman's record spans junior success, three British titles, major international tournament victories, two Candidates appearances, repeated Olympiad medals and several decades of work as an author and analyst, making him one of the most significant figures in modern English chess.

Jon Speelman's Agony column

With his usual wit and analytic depth, Jon has been writing regular columns on our news site for a number of years now. In fact, his latest instalment, published a couple of weeks ago was the 243rd. Find below links to a few of his best columns or go over all his pieces on the author's page .

#132: When 3 is greater than 5

Jon Speelman explores the exchange sacrifice. Speelman shares five illustrative examples to explain in which conditions giving up a rook for a minor piece is a good trade. "As a general rule and in fact (almost all?) of the time you need other pieces on the board for an exchange sacrifice to work".

#147: Overthinking the silence

Often times during a chess game you have to make a choice between waiting and initiating concrete action. Star columnist Jon Speelman notes that "this eerie silence before battle is perhaps the most difficult moment psychologically", and goes on to show how even world champion Magnus Carlsen can take a wrong turn from time to time.

#196: Seeing the whole board

When a strong player looks at a position (in a real game of chess, not a problem) he or she will automatically see it not as a random collection of pieces but as a series of chunks - patterns that are recognisable and have known features. And the patterns will also generate ideas of moves which may be profitable. Curiously, sometimes apparently insignificant changes can be crucial, and today I’m focussing on an instance of this phenomenon.

#215: The search for less than perfection (or when -0.07 > 0.11)

One of the most interesting aspects of the Candidates Tournament was the superb opening preparation, and in particular how they managed to set each other problems which hadn't been foreseen. This is a special skill that involves interacting with the fearsome engines not to find the "best" moves but ones which are almost as strong according to the silicon evaluation - but lower down the food chain!

#237: Battles with Jan

Jon Speelman reflects on the career and personality of Dutch GM Jan Timman following the news of his passing. Speelman recalls their encounters over the board, including games from their 1989 Candidates' match in London. "Away from the board, Jan was always excellent company and I always thought that he was one of the very nicest of the generation just a few years older than me".

title: Is Russia plotting to kill Kasparov?
summary:
According to reports in several media outlets, Garry Kasparov was among a number of Russian dissidents abroad targeted in an alleged Russian assassination plot. As first reported by the Spanish newspaper El Mundo, US prosecutors have charged five people accused of working for Russian intelligence services to plan attacks on Russian opposition figures and carry out acts of sabotage.

Kasparov was reportedly warned by US and Lithuanian security services this summer that he could be among the targets of planned attacks on Russian exiles. He and his wife were subsequently placed under protection. The US indictment itself does not identify Kasparov by name.

Another reported target was former Russian MP Ilya Ponomarev, who was the only one of 450 members of the State Duma to vote against Russia's annexation of Crimea. In 2014, after travelling to the United States, Ponomarev did not return to Russia because he feared for his life. He moved to Ukraine in 2016 and, after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, spent some time fighting alongside Ukrainian forces. More recently, he has divided his time between Ukraine and the United States.

Kasparov had already decided not to return to Russia after travelling abroad in 2013. The former World Champion, who became active in the Russian opposition after retiring from professional chess, feared for his life. Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Russian authorities designated Kasparov a "foreign agent" and later added him to their list of "terrorists and extremists". In May 2026, a Russian court issued an international arrest warrant for him.

Vladimir Kara-Murza has also been mentioned as a possible target. The Russian opposition politician survived two suspected poisonings and was later imprisoned in Siberia. In 2024, he was released as part of a major prisoner exchange involving Russian agents.

According to El Mundo, the alleged network is led by Yuri Khrameev, a former colonel in the Russian intelligence services. His son Kirill, an FSB officer, is also accused of belonging to the network, along with Cuban nationals Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez and Venezuelan national Angel Eduardo Castro. US prosecutors say the five worked for Russian intelligence services, recruiting people to conduct surveillance and targeted killings as well as acts of sabotage. All five are believed to be in Russia and remain at large.

The network is also alleged to have planned the murder of Ivan Tyutrin, a Russian opposition activist living in Lithuania who co-founded the Free Russia Forum with Kasparov in 2016. Russian authorities designated the organization "undesirable" in 2023 and added it to their list of "terrorist organizations" in 2025.

Russian intelligence services have previously been accused of attacks on opponents and defectors in Europe. Among the best-known cases are the 2018 Novichok poisoning of former GRU officer Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia in Salisbury, which both survived; the 2019 murder of Chechen-Georgian dissident Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in Berlin; and the 2024 killing in Spain of Russian helicopter pilot Maxim Kuzminov, who had defected to Ukraine.

The United States, however, had largely been avoided as a venue for such operations. The new US indictment alleges that members of the network recruited people inside the United States to surveil Russian dissidents and carry out killings. If proven, the case would mark a significant expansion of such operations onto US soil.

My thanks to everyone expressing their outrage and concern. Of course there are millions of people whose lives are threatened by Russia every day in Ukraine, and Ukrainian victory remains the best form of security for me, my colleagues, and all of Europe. https://t.co/LjPmoZTeY8

— Garry Kasparov (@Kasparov63) September 30, 2026

title: Nepo has dragon problems - The Monthly Dragon
summary:
The Monthly Dragon

with GM Chris Ward

The British Grandmaster Chris Ward is always delighted if he can play his favourite opening as Black: the Sicilian Dragon.

Ward's knowledge about this strong opening is covered in several of his books , his blog on chesspublishing and his three, greatly popular FritzTrainers in our ChessBase shop .

With the new ChessBase series "The Monthly Dragon", the passionate Salsa dancer is showing us the newest tactics, plans and development of this fascinating opening.

Lucky for us, the dragon is an opening, played by some of the best players in the world. This means, Chris probably won't run out of fuel for new content.
